title: REF: Reduce cognitive complexity of `tokenize_bytes`
body:
The [`tokenize_bytes`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/15b1dd913e3df72854955936b0d89c7f95648a9a/pandas/_libs/src/parser/tokenizer.c#L779-L1357) function currently has a cognitive complexity score of 551 according to `clang-tidy`, which significantly exceeds the default threshold of 25.

The complexity primarily comes from managing 16 distinct parser states within a single monolithic loop, combined with inline SIMD preprocessing and scalar fallback logic. Modularizing the state handling into smaller helper functions would help improve the readability and long-term maintainability of the CSV parser.

title: BUG: False ChainedAssignmentError, misattributed to the caller, when setitem runs in Cython-compiled code — and no supported way to disable the check
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


Two files. `repro_mod.py` contains only a plain, legal column assignment on
a function-local DataFrame — no mask, no intermediate object, no second
subscript:

```python
# repro_mod.py
import pandas as pd


def legal_assignment():
    df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
    df["b"] = df["a"] * 2
    return df

```
```python
# run_repro.py
import warnings

import pandas as pd

import repro_mod

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    df = repro_mod.legal_assignment()

assert df["b"].tolist() == [2, 4, 6]  # the assignment itself worked fine

chained = [w for w in caught
           if issubclass(w.category, pd.errors.ChainedAssignmentError)]

if not chained:
    print("OK: no warning")
else:
    for w in chained:
        print(f"FALSE POSITIVE: {w.category.__name__} "
              f"attributed to {w.filename}:{w.lineno}")
```

Run it twice — once with the module as plain Python, once after compiling
that same module into a C extension with Cython:

```shell
$ python run_repro.py
```
OK: no warning

$ cythonize -3 -i repro_mod.py
$ python run_repro.py

title: PERF: union_indexes is slow for homogeneous RangeIndexes during DataFrame concatenation
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Concatenating many small DataFrames with homogeneous (often identical) columns or index `RangeIndex` objects spends significant time in `union_indexes` and `RangeIndex.union`. 

For example, when concatenating 2,000 small DataFrames along `axis=0` with identical columns, `union_indexes` is called on a list of 2,000 `RangeIndex(0, 10)` objects. Currently, this performs a loop of 1,999 sequential `result.union(other)` calls, which incurs high type check, name reconciliation (`_get_reconciled_name_object`), and new index object creation overhead (consuming over 50% of the runtime).

### Reproducible Example
```python
import pandas as pd
import time

# 2,000 small DataFrames with identical columns
dfs = [pd.DataFrame(0, index=[i], columns=pd.RangeIndex(0, 10)) for i in range(2000)]

t0 = time.perf_counter()
pd.concat(dfs)
t1 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"Concatenation time: {t1 - t0:.4f} seconds")
```

### Proposed Solution
Add a fast-path inside `union_indexes` when all input indices are `RangeIndex` instances:

- Deduplicate them quickly using a set of (range, name) tuples.
- If all unique non-empty indices share the same step and name, check if they are contiguous/overlapping (no gaps).
- If they are contiguous, directly return a single `RangeIndex` spanning the start/stop range.
- Otherwise, fall back to the standard union logic but only iterate over the deduplicated unique `RangeIndexes`.

title: BUG:  `cummax` / `cummin` incorrect for pyarrow floating dtypes
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([-4.0, -3.0, -2.0, -1.0], dtype="float64[pyarrow]")
print(s.cummax())
```

### Issue Description

`Series.cummax()` / `DataFrame.cummax()` on a pyarrow floating dtype ( `float32[pyarrow]` / `float64[pyarrow]` ) silently returns a tiny sentinel (~2.2e-308, which prints as 0.0) instead of the true running maximum whenever the running max is negative (or zero/subnormal), because the underlying `pyarrow.compute.cumulative_max` call omits start, so pyarrow defaults it to the smallest positive float instead of `-inf`. The same root cause makes `cummin` return a wrong value when the running min is `+inf` 

### Expected Behavior

`cummax` should return the true running maximum (e.g. [-4, -3, -2, -1] for [-4, -3, -2, -1]), matching the numpy-backed dtype, instead of 0.0.

title: CI: Unpin CI dependencies
body:
With the release of `pytest` 9.1.1, the `pytest<9.1` pin in [`unit-tests.yml`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/ead0d998c4672966991c0380ba7a65e522c16355/.github/workflows/unit-tests.yml) is no longer needed.

Additionally, the `meson` pin prevents us from using new Meson features, such as the NumPy dependency (xref #63703). AFAIU, it was pinned to prevent warnings from failing builds under `-Werror`. It's possible to unpin it and handle any resulting warnings using specific `-Wno-...` flags instead.

title: Consider adding a changelog to track version history
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
A `CHANGELOG.md` file would help users understand what changed between versions and make upgrade decisions easier.

### Motivation
When upgrading dependencies, developers need to know:
- What bugs were fixed
- What new features were added
- Whether there are any breaking changes

### Suggested Format
Follow the [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com) convention:

```markdown
# Changelog

## [Unreleased]

## [1.2.0] - 2024-01-15
### Added
- New feature X
### Fixed  
- Bug with Y under Z conditions
### Changed
- Behaviour of Z is now more consistent
```

### Additional Context
This is purely a documentation change with no code impact.

title: PERF: High overhead in stack frame warning inspections (find_stack_level)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Whenever pandas raises a warning, it invokes `find_stack_level()` to trace the call stack and identify the calling context outside of pandas. Currently, this function walks the stack frames and calls `inspect.getfile(frame)` inside a loop:

```python
while frame:
    filename = inspect.getfile(frame)
    if filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir):
        frame = frame.f_back
        n += 1
```

For workloads that emit multiple warnings (or libraries relying heavily on pandas warnings), this function is highly inefficient because:
1. `inspect.getfile(frame)` is slow as it does lookup caching, module parsing, and absolute path validation inside the interpreter loop.
2. It repeatedly imports `pandas` and resolves `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths on *every* warning invocation.

### Proposed Optimization
1. Cache the `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths globally at the module level.
2. Retrieve the filename directly via `frame.f_code.co_filename` instead of calling `inspect.getfile(frame)`.

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked 500,000 runs of the original stack inspection vs. the optimized caching and `co_filename` check on a local environment:

| Implementation | 500,000 runs | Overhead per call |
|---|---|---|
| **Original (`master`)** | 3.67 seconds | ~7.33 microseconds |
| **Optimized** | 0.19 seconds | ~0.38 microseconds |

This yields a **~19x speedup** (95% reduction in call overhead).

title: PERF: String column serialization in Interchange protocol is slow
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


### Problem Description
Currently, when serializing string columns to a byte buffer in the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas uses a slow element-wise Python loop:

```python
for obj in buf:
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        b.extend(obj.encode(encoding="utf-8"))
```

For large DataFrames ($100k+$ or $1M+$ rows), this loop is highly inefficient because:
1. It calls `.encode("utf-8")` once for every single string element inside the Python interpreter.
2. It uses `bytearray.extend()` iteratively, introducing overhead.
3. The check `isinstance(obj, str)` is run iteratively in Python.

### Proposed Optimization
We can leverage NumPy to filter nulls/invalid elements in C-space and then perform a single C-optimized join and a single vectorized `.encode()` call:

```python
# Drop null values to avoid joining None/NaN
b = "".join(buf[pd.notna(buf)]).encode(encoding="utf-8")
```

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked the original loop logic vs. the optimized NumPy mask & join approach on array sizes with 5% missing values:

| Size (Strings) | Original Loop | Optimized Python | Speedup Factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **10,000** | 0.00530s | 0.00227s | **2.34x** |
| **100,000** | 0.06940s | 0.02344s | **2.96x** |
| **1,000,000** | 0.22295s | 0.10143s | **2.20x** |

title: BUG: CustomBusinessMonthBegin and CustomBusinessMonthEnd type signatures are missing the calendar and weekmask keyword arguments
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

cal = np.busdaycalendar()

pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin(calendar=cal)
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd(calendar=cal)
```

### Issue Description

## Description

The type signatures for `CustomBusinessMonthBegin` and `CustomBusinessMonthEnd` are missing the `calendar` and `weekmask` keyword arguments, even though they are supported at runtime and documented.

By comparison, `CustomBusinessDay` correctly exposes the `calendar` parameter in its type signature.

As a result, valid code fails type checking with mypy.

## Reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

cal = np.busdaycalendar()

pd.offsets.CustomBusinessDay(calendar=cal)          # OK
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin(calendar=cal)   # mypy error
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd(calendar=cal)     # mypy error
```

mypy reports:

```text
error: Unexpected keyword argument "calendar" for "CustomBusinessMonthBegin"  [call-arg]
error: Unexpected keyword argument "calendar" for "CustomBusinessMonthEnd"  [call-arg]
```

```python
from pandas.tseries.offsets import (
    CustomBusinessDay,
    CustomBusinessMonthBegin,

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [4, 5, 6], "C": [7, 8, 9]})

title: Add type hints to public API functions
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
Adding type hints to public API functions would significantly improve developer experience and enable better tooling support.

### Motivation
- IDEs can provide better autocomplete and inline documentation
- Static type checkers like `mypy` can catch bugs before runtime
- New contributors can understand the expected inputs/outputs faster
- Type hints serve as machine-checked documentation

### Proposed Change
Add type annotations to all public functions:

```python
# Before:
def process(data, config=None):
    ...

# After:
from typing import Optional, Dict, Any

def process(data: Dict[str, Any], config: Optional[Dict] = None) -> bool:
    ...
```

### Additional Context
This is a non-breaking change and can be done incrementally, starting with the most-used public functions.

title: BUG: pd.date_range(freq='h') produces astronomically large freq on Python 3.14, causing OverflowError
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/v3.0.4.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
print(pd.__version__)   # 3.0.4
print(pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h"))
```

### Issue Description

On **pandas 3.0.4 + Python 3.14**, `pd.date_range(..., freq="h")` raises an `OverflowError` / `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`. The `freq` argument is silently reinterpreted as an astronomically large `Hours` offset (e.g. `<281467879224592 * Hours>`) instead of `<1 * Hours>`.

The same call works correctly on **pandas 3.0.3 + Python 3.14**.

### Full traceback

```
pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.pyx:2014: OverflowError

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

start = Timestamp('2026-04-17 00:00:00'), end = None, periods = 24
freq = <281467879224592 * Hours>, unit = 'us'

    def generate_regular_range(...):
        ...
        try:
            td = td.as_unit(unit, round_ok=False)
        except ValueError as err:
            raise ValueError(
                f"freq={freq} is incompatible with unit={unit}. "
                "Use a lower freq or a higher unit instead."
            ) from err

pandas/core/arrays/_ranges.py:74: ValueError:
  freq=<281467879224592 * Hours> is incompatible with unit=us.

```

Also observed as:

```
pandas.errors.OutOfBoundsTimedelta:
  Cannot cast 11727828301024 days 16:00:00 to unit='us' without overflow.
```

### Expected Behavior

`pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h")` should return a `DatetimeIndex` of 24 hourly timestamps, as it does on pandas 3.0.3.

### Installed Versions

- pandas: **3.0.4** (regression; **3.0.3** works)
- Python: **3.14.6**

### Reproducible Example

In a fresh virtualenv with **only** `pandas==3.0.4` (and its required deps `numpy`, `python-dateutil`) installed on **CPython 3.14**:

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Timedelta(days=28)   # Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
```

Any `Timedelta` constructor crashes the interpreter at construction time — `pd.Timedelta(days=28)`, `pd.Timedelta("28 days")`, `pd.Timedelta(28, "D")`. No DataFrame/Series is involved, no threading, single-threaded `python -c`.

### Issue Description

Constructing a `pandas.Timedelta` segfaults immediately on **pandas 3.0.4 / CPython 3.14**. This is a **regression from 3.0.3** — in the same virtualenv, downgrading only `pandas` (`3.0.4` → `3.0.3`, numpy unchanged) makes the example work, and upgrading back to `3.0.4` crashes again. So `pandas` is the only changed variable.

It reproduces with numpy **2.3.3** (pandas 3.0.4's own declared minimum for Python 3.14, `numpy>=2.3.3`) and with numpy **2.4.6**, so it is not specific to a single numpy build.

With `PYTHONFAULTHANDLER=1`, the C stack shows what looks like unbounded recursion between `pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas` and numpy's `_multiarray_umath`, overflowing the C stack:

title: BUG: Segfault constructing pd.Timedelta with numpy 2.3.x/2.4.x on Python 3.14 (pandas 3.0.4)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas (3.0.4).

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.Timedelta(1, unit="D")   # interpreter exits with SIGSEGV (signal 11)
```

`import pandas` succeeds; `numpy.timedelta64(1, "D")` succeeds; the **first**
`pd.Timedelta(...)` construction crashes the interpreter. No Python traceback is
produced.

### Issue Description

On Python 3.14, `pandas==3.0.4` segfaults when constructing a `Timedelta` if the
installed numpy is in the 2.3.x–2.4.x range. The crash is a hard SIGSEGV
(exit 139), single-process and fully deterministic.

The numpy `_multiarray_umath` shared object is not stripped, so the faulting
frame symbolizes exactly:

```
#0  PyUFunc_f_f (numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so + 0xd5f58)
        => mov (%rdx),%r15            # registers at fault: rdx = 0x6, rcx = 0x0
#1  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#2  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#3  slot_tp_new -> type_call -> _PyObject_MakeTpCall    # Timedelta(1, unit='D')
```

`PyUFunc_f_f` is numpy's generic float32 unary ufunc inner loop, whose signature
is `(char **args, npy_intp *dimensions, npy_intp *steps, void *func)`. At the
fault, `rdx` (the `steps` pointer) holds `0x6` and `rcx` (`func`) is `NULL`; the
loop dereferences `steps` and segfaults.

I bisected across numpy/pandas versions, each in a clean venv (Python 3.14.5),
running only the one-liner above:

| numpy  | pandas | result  |
|--------|--------|---------|
| 2.3.5  | 3.0.3  | OK      |
| 2.3.5  | 3.0.4  | SIGSEGV |
| 2.4.6  | 3.0.4  | SIGSEGV |
| 2.5.0  | 3.0.4  | OK      |

Observations (reporting only, not asserting a cause):

- pandas 3.0.3 and 3.0.4 both declare `numpy>=2.3.3; python_version >= "3.14"`.
  3.0.3 runs fine on numpy 2.3.5; 3.0.4 segfaults on the same numpy.

title: BUG: Series.str.match returns wrong result for ^a|b patterns on string[pyarrow] dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
python 

import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["xbar", "bar", "foo", "xfoo"])

print("Actual:  ", s.str.match(r"^foo|bar").tolist())
print("Expected:", s.astype(object).str.match(r"^foo|bar").tolist())





Output 
Actual:   [True, True, True, False]
Expected: [False, True, True, False]
```

### Issue Description

`Series.str.match(r"^foo|bar")` on the default (PyArrow-backed) string dtype silently returns True for "xbar" (matches "bar" at position 1 instead of requiring it at position 0), because the ^ only anchors the first alternation branch.

Object dtype (and `re.match`) anchors the whole pattern at position 0 and correctly returns False, so this is a silent regression for users on pandas 3.x with PyArrow installed.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.str.match(pat)` should anchor the entire pattern at position 0 (matching Python's `re.match` and the object-dtype behavior), so `r"^foo|bar"` should only return `True` for strings that start with `"foo"` or `"bar"`.

title: DataFrame constructed from Index or Series mutates the original object
body:
# BUG: `DataFrame` constructed from `Index` or `Series` mutates the original object

## Description

When constructing a `DataFrame` from a pandas `Index` or `Series` containing string data, any modifications made to the new `DataFrame` unexpectedly mutate the original `Index` or `Series`. This occurs even when `.copy()` is explicitly called before passing the object to the constructor — the underlying array is reused rather than being independently tracked.

This bug does **not** affect integer-backed `Index` or `Series` objects, only string (and other extension array) types.

Additionally, this can break internal invariants — displaying a `DataFrame` whose columns were modified this way has been observed to crash the IPython kernel.

## Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# Bug with Index input
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
columns = pd.DataFrame(data=df.columns.copy())
columns.loc[0, 0] = 'C'
assert df.columns[0] == 'A'  # FAILS — original Index was mutated

# Bug with string Index directly
idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"])
df2 = pd.DataFrame(idx)
df2.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(idx)  # Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original mutated

# Bug with string Series input
ser = pd.Series(["A", "B"])
df3 = pd.DataFrame(ser)
df3.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(ser)  # 0    C \n 1    B — original mutated

# No bug with integer Index (works correctly)
idx_int = pd.Index([0, 1])
df4 = pd.DataFrame(idx_int)
df4.iloc[0, 0] = 100
print(idx_int)  # Index([0, 1], dtype='int64') — unchanged
```

## Expected Behavior

```python
idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"])
df = pd.DataFrame(idx)
df.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(idx)  # Expected: Index(['A', 'B'], dtype='str') — unchanged
```

## Actual Behavior

```python
print(idx)  # Actual: Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original was silently mutated
```

```

numpy      : 2.3.5
python     : 3.11.14

If you build a `DataFrame` from an `Index` or `Series` backed by an Extension Array, CoW reference tracking is missing. The result is that mutating the new `DataFrame` can silently change the original `Index` — which obviously shouldn't happen.

### Expected Behavior

`df.columns` shouldn't be affected at all. CoW means either copy the data upfront or track the reference and copy on first write — neither is happening here.

title: Add logging support for better observability
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
The project would benefit from structured logging to make it easier to debug issues in production.

### Motivation
Currently it can be difficult to understand what the application is doing at runtime without adding print statements. Proper logging would:

- Allow users to control verbosity with log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)
- Make it easier to integrate with log aggregation systems
- Help diagnose issues in production without code changes

### Proposed Implementation
```python
import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def my_function():
    log.debug("Starting my_function")
    # ... 
    log.info("my_function completed successfully")
```

### Impact
Low risk change with high value for users running this in production environments.

title: Potential resource leak when exception occurs during file operation
body:
## Bug Report

### Description
When an exception is raised during a file operation, the file handle may not be properly closed, leading to a resource leak.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Open a file without using a context manager
2. Raise an exception before closing the file
3. The file handle remains open

### Expected Behavior
File handles should always be closed, even when exceptions occur.

### Suggested Fix
Use a `with` statement (context manager) to ensure the file is always closed:

```python
# Instead of:
f = open('file.txt', 'r')
data = f.read()
f.close()

# Use:
with open('file.txt', 'r') as f:
    data = f.read()
```

### Environment
- Python 3.x
- Any OS

This is a common Python pitfall that can cause issues in long-running applications.

title: BUG: missing deprecation warning about epoch timestamps in the index in to_json()
body:
When we have a datetime64 column and writing to JSON, we get a warning about the default "epoch" `date_format` being deprecated. 
However, when the datetime64 data is in the index, we don't get the warning, while we also get epoch values:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [pd.Timestamp("2012-01-01"), pd.Timestamp("2012-01-02")]})
>>> df.to_json()
Pandas4Warning: The default 'epoch' date format is deprecated and will be removed in a future version, please use 'iso' date format instead.
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":1325376000000,"1":1325462400000}}'

>>> df.set_index("B").to_json()    # <-- no warning
'{"A":{"1325376000000":1,"1325462400000":2}}'
```

Both cases work fine with `date_format="iso"`:

```python
>>> df.to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000","1":"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000"}}'
>>> df.set_index("B").to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000":1,"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000":2}}'
```

But so if we want to be able to change to `"iso"` by default in 4.0 for both cases, we also have to warn now in both cases

GH-29461 / PR GH-64899 added a `%N` directive to `Timestamp.strftime` and the
array-level `strftime`, formatting nanoseconds as a 9-digit zero-padded number.
The parsing side does not accept it, so `%N` output doesn't round-trip with the
same format string:

```python
>>> ts = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-14 15:32:52.192548651")
>>> fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N"
>>> pd.to_datetime(ts.strftime(fmt), format=fmt)
ValueError: 'N' is a bad directive in format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N'
```

Note that pandas' strptime already parses nanoseconds via `%f` (it accepts 1-9
digits, an extension over the stdlib's 6), so this is about symmetry and
round-tripping rather than new capability. Suggested in
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64899#pullrequestreview-4481273478.

### Feature Description

Accept `%N` in `format=` for `to_datetime`, `Timestamp`, and related parsing
paths, matching exactly 9 digits (vs `%f`'s 1-9). Likely just an entry next to
`"f"` in the `TimeRE` class and corresponding handling in `strptime.pyx`.

### Alternative Solutions

Keep parsing via `%f`, which already handles 9 digits — but then a format
string built for `%N` output can't be reused for parsing.

### Additional Context

`Period.strftime` has long supported `%n`/`%N` for formatting only; linux
`date` uses `%N` for nanoseconds.

title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow engine) opens the local file path twice
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import builtins
import os

import pandas as pd

# Spy on Python-level opens of the destination path.
target = "test.parquet"
opens = []
real_open = builtins.open

def spy_open(file, *args, **kwargs):
    if os.path.abspath(os.fspath(file)) == os.path.abspath(target):
        opens.append(args)
    return real_open(file, *args, **kwargs)

builtins.open = spy_open
try:
    pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}).to_parquet(target, engine="pyarrow")
finally:
    builtins.open = real_open

print(f"pandas opened the destination {len(opens)} time(s) at the Python level")

# Observed: 1  -> pandas opens the file itself via get_handle...
# ...but pyarrow ALSO opens the same path through its C++ layer and does the
# actual writing, so the path is opened twice per to_parquet call.

# On Linux this is also visible at the syscall level:
# strace -f -e trace=openat python -c \
#  "import pandas as pd; pd.DataFrame({'a':[1]}).to_parquet('x.parquet')" 2>&1 \
#  | grep -c 'x.parquet'
# two openat() calls for the same path
```

### Issue Description

For a local filesystem path, `to_parquet` with the pyarrow engine resolves the path through `pandas.io.common.get_handle` inside `_get_path_or_handle`, then unwraps the handle's .name back to a string and hands that string to pyarrow. pyarrow then opens  the same path a second time through its own (memory-mapped, multithreaded) C++ I/O layer, which is where the read/write actually happens. So every local-path call opens the destination/source twice.

Consequences:
- On POSIX: a wasted `open()`/`close()` syscall

### Reproducible Example

We actually noticed the slowness from `pandas.read_sql`, but narrowed the problem down to its call to `has_table`. We're calling `read_sql` with a query so it will always be a miss for `has_table`.

```python
import time
import pandas.io.sql as pd_sql
from adbc_driver_snowflake.dbapi import connect

with connect("<database URI>") as conn:  # Connection to a large database
    start = time.perf_counter()
    pd_sql.has_table("foo", conn)  # Where foo does not match a table
    end = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"Took {end - start} seconds")
```

The problem sees to be in [`pandas.io.sql.ADBCDatabase.has_table`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/sql.py#L2429-L2431), which calls [`self.con.adbc_get_objects()`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/python/api/adbc_driver_manager.html#adbc_driver_manager.dbapi.Connection.adbc_get_objects) without passing `depth=`. body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

# Problem Description
Currently, when users attempt to access a column that does not exist in a DataFrame using:

df["Age"]

Pandas raises a generic error message:

KeyError: 'Age'

While technically correct, this message provides very limited context for users, especially beginners.

The current behavior does not:

explain why the error occurred,
show available columns,
help users identify possible typos,
improve debugging experience.

This can make debugging slower and more frustrating for new users working with DataFrames.

Example Reproduction
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Pradip", "Rahul"]
})

print(df["Age"])

Current output:

KeyError: 'Age'

# Expected Behavior

The error message should provide more contextual information.

Possible improved output:

KeyError: Column 'Age' not found in DataFrame.
Available columns: ['Name']

OR:

KeyError: Column 'Age' does not exist.
Did you mean: 'Name'?

### Feature Description

# Feature Description

Enhance the DataFrame column-access error handling mechanism to produce more descriptive and user-friendly error messages when a requested column is missing.

Potential improvements include:

  1.displaying available column names,
  2.suggesting similar column names,
  3.clarifying that the requested column does not exist,
  4.improving beginner usability.

This enhancement would improve:

  debugging experience,
  developer productivity,
  accessibility for new Pandas users.

### Alternative Solutions

# Proposed Solution

Locate the internal column access logic (likely in:

pandas/core/frame.py

)

and replace the generic:

raise KeyError(key)

with a more informative exception message.

Example:

raise KeyError(
    f"Column '{key}' not found in DataFrame. "
    f"Available columns: {list(self.columns)}"
)

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

a = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3, 4], mask=[False, True, False, True])

# BUG: mask is ignored completely
pd.array(a)
# Output:
# <IntegerArray>
# [1, 2, 3, 4]
# Length: 4, dtype: Int64

# For comparison, pd.Series handles the mask but changes dtype to float
pd.Series(a)
# Output:
# 0 1.0
# 1 NaN
# 2 3.0
# 3 NaN
# dtype: float64
```

### Issue Description

NumPy [masked arrays](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/maskedarray.generic.html#what-is-a-masked-array) are used to define arrays with missing values, similar to pandas extension arrays. However, converting to `pd.array` currently ignores the mask completely and masked values appear as regular values.

Converting to `pd.Series` does respect the missing values, but the dtype is converted to `float` and the original dtype is not preserved in all cases.

This behavior is inconsistent with user expectations and with how `pd.Series` handles masked arrays.

The same issue occurs with string masked arrays where the mask is also ignored by `pd.array`.

### Expected Behavior

Masked values should be converted to pd.NA and the appropriate nullable dtype should be preserved, such as Int64 or string, instead of ignoring the mask or coercing to float.

>>> pd.array(a)
<IntegerArray>
[1, <NA>, 3, <NA>]
Length: 4, dtype: Int64

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ONE_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Budapest")
OTHER_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Moscow")

# Example (works): different timezones, no NaT
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, OTHER_TZ]})
df1.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (works): same timezone, with NaT
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[ONE_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df2.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (fails): different timezone, with NaT
df3 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df3.max(axis=1) # Fails, as soon as we have a NaT
```

### Issue Description

In dataframes with datetime64 columns, max() fails with a `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'` when 2 different timezones and NaT values are both present. As long as we have 1 timezone or no NaTs, everything works as expected. The default behavior of max() is skipping nans, and NaT is interpreted as such correctly with the same timezone. Once the timezone is different, it is treated as a float and the comparison fails.

It seems like during the max() operation, since timezones differ, rows are coerced into an `object` dtype. The NaT is leaking into the underlying numpy amax as a float instead of being safely skipped or masked out before the comparison occurs.

### Expected Behavior

Truly skipping NaTs as a default in max() before attempting the comparison of the remaining datetime64 values.

title: PERF: skip redundant Index.equals calls in pd.concat
body:
### Problem

`pd.concat` compares the same logical pair of indexes twice:

1. `union_indexes` → `all_indexes_same` (`indexes/api.py:337`) walks the inputs pairwise (`first.equals(idx)` for each other), and returns `indexes[0]` when they all match.
2. Then `_get_result` (`reshape/concat.py:652`) re-runs `new_labels.equals(obj_labels)` per obj to decide whether reindexing is needed — re-asking the same question.

In the common case where input frames are separately-constructed with content-equal-but-identity-distinct column indexes, ~50% of all `Index.equals` calls under `pd.concat` are this duplicate.

### Numbers (per call, inputs pre-built outside the timer)

| workload | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 0.62 ms | 0.50 ms | **1.25x** |
| 1000 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 6.76 ms | 5.70 ms | 1.19x |
| 100 frames, 20 cols, multi-block (dict-built) | 0.64 ms | 0.49 ms | **1.31x** |
| 20 sibling-tables, axis=1, 1000 rows | 0.19 ms | 0.15 ms | 1.25x |
| 200 frames built fresh + concat (read-many-files) | 7.96 ms | 7.58 ms | 1.05x |

"After" estimated by short-circuiting duplicate `(id(self), id(other))` pairs with a per-concat memoization cache.

### Beneficiary

Patterns that build frames separately then concat them: `pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in files])` and equivalents.

`groupby.apply` and `pd.concat([df.iloc[a:b] for ...])` see **zero** `Index.equals` calls (slices share the parent's Index identity, `_get_distinct_objs` collapses them) — this change is a no-op for those.

### Proposed change

Return an `all_equal` flag from `union_indexes` when it takes the `all_indexes_same`-True branch, and thread it through `_get_combined_index` → `new_axes` → `_get_result`. When True, `_get_result` skips the per-obj `equals` and uses empty indexers.

Happy to put up a PR.

title: PERF: cache BlockManager.get_dtypes() result
body:
### Problem

`BaseBlockManager.get_dtypes()` (`pandas/core/internals/managers.py:339`) rebuilds an object array on every call:

```python
def get_dtypes(self) -> npt.NDArray[np.object_]:
    dtypes = np.array([blk.dtype for blk in self.blocks], dtype=object)
    return dtypes.take(self.blknos)
```

It's called from a number of hot paths — `df.dtypes`, `DataFrame.fillna` (`generic.py:6391`), `select_dtypes`/`_get_numeric_data`, `DataFrame.apply` (`frame.py:15751`), `unique_dtypes` in repr/info (`generic.py:7136`), and twice per `iloc` setitem (`indexing.py:944, 975`). For wide, fragmented managers each call is O(nblocks) Python iteration plus an object-array allocation.

### Numbers (1000-col DataFrame, 335 blocks, mixed f8/i8/object)

| call | current | with cache | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mgr.get_dtypes()` | 47 us | 0.08 us | **608x** |
| `df.dtypes` | 58 us | 8.7 us | **6.7x** |

Caching saves the full cost on cache hits; `df.dtypes` retains ~8 us of unavoidable Series-construction overhead.

### Proposed change

Add a `_dtypes_cache` attribute on the manager, populated lazily in `get_dtypes()` and invalidated alongside the existing `_blknos` / `_interleaved_dtype` cache hooks (`managers.py:1411, 1497` and other block-mutation sites). The same invalidation pattern is already in place — adding one more entry is mechanical.

### Caveats

- The cached array must not be mutated in place by callers. A quick audit of callers shows they only read it (equality checks, `.take`, iteration) — no in-place writes — but worth confirming during review.
- `SingleBlockManager` already has only one block; the cache is still cheap and consistent.

Happy to put up a PR.

title: PERF: skip to_datetime cache=True overhead for input shapes where it cannot help
body:
#### Summary

`to_datetime(..., cache=True)` (the default) unconditionally runs the
`_maybe_cache` machinery — `Series(dtype=object)` construction +
`should_cache` which iterates up to 500 elements of the input — even on
inputs where `_convert_listlike_datetimes` is going to dispatch to a
non-parsing path or a path where caching has been measured to never help.
On these inputs `cache=True` is strictly slower than `cache=False`, by
margins ranging from a few percent to **~520×** at the worst.

All five "no-help" conditions are identifiable in O(1) time, before any
sampling, just by looking at `arg.dtype`, the `unit` kwarg, and the
`format` kwarg.

#### Affected input shapes (all O(1) to detect)

1. `unit is not None` — input is dispatched to `_to_datetime_with_unit`,
   which is a vectorized cast; caching cannot help.
2. `arg.dtype` is `np.dtype("M8[*]")` — already datetime64; `_convert_listlike_datetimes` short-circuits.
3. `arg.dtype` is `DatetimeTZDtype` — already tz-aware; short-circuits.
4. `arg.dtype` is `ArrowDtype` with `type is Timestamp` — short-circuits.
5. `format is not None and format != "mixed"` — `array_strptime` is fast
   enough that `pd.unique()` + `Series.map()` costs as much as just
   re-parsing; `cache=True` is never a measurable win on this path.

#### Reproducer

```python

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def best(fn, k=5):
    fn()  # warmup
    times = []
    for _ in range(k):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return min(times)


def bench(label, arg, **kwargs):
    t_off = best(lambda: pd.to_datetime(arg, cache=False, **kwargs))
    t_on = best(lambda: pd.to_datetime(arg, cache=True, **kwargs))

title: ENH: pd.crosstab with normalize='index' and margins=True drops the marginal 'Total' column.
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

When creating a contingency table using pd.crosstab, if a user specifies normalize='index' while also requesting margins=True, the resulting DataFrame includes the marginal row (at the bottom) but excludes the marginal column (on the right). While the marginal column would mathematically consist of constants (1.0), its omission prevents the generation of a complete "framed" table for reporting and visualization purposes.

It is normal in data science to display both row and column totals in a crosstab.  If you select row or column as the sum, it's expect to show 100% on the non-selected column,  this is supported by the grand total selection where only the total in the bottom right is 100%.  This helps users quick understand what you are trying to convey and reinforces the choice of display 

The default should be to hide the result which is 1.0

### Feature Description

def _add_margins(self, table, margins_name):
    # CURRENT BEHAVIOR: 
    # Pandas calculates the sum of columns and rows.
    # If normalize='index', the row sum is always 1.0.
    
    # PROPOSED FIX:
    # Explicitly check if normalize is 'index' or 'columns' 
    # to prevent the 'Total' column/row from being optimized away.

    if self.normalize == 'index':
        # Force add the marginal column of 1.0s
        table[margins_name] = 1.0 
        
        # Calculate the marginal row (the distribution of the columns)
        # This is the mean of the normalized rows or a separate total calculation
        column_totals = table.iloc[:, :-1].mean(axis=0) 
        table.loc[margins_name] = column_totals
        table.at[margins_name, margins_name] = 1.0
        
    return table

none

- Code Checks / Docstring validation, typing, and other manual pre-commit hooks

title: API: Index.take discards fill_value and raises unnecessarily
body:
`Index.take` has two bugs when `allow_fill=True` and `fill_value` is passed explicitly:

### 1. `fill_value` is silently discarded

The caller's `fill_value` is ignored; `self._na_value` is always substituted:

```python
# Note: we discard fill_value and use self._na_value, only relevant
#  in the case where allow_fill is True and fill_value is not None
taken = algos.take(
    values, indices, allow_fill=allow_fill, fill_value=self._na_value
)
```

### 2. `_can_hold_na` gate raises on integer dtypes

```python
>>> pd.Index([1, 2, 3]).take([0, -1], allow_fill=True, fill_value=99)
ValueError: Unable to fill values because Index cannot contain NA
```

The caller provided a valid fill value that the dtype can hold, but `Index.take` rejects it because `_can_hold_na` is False for integer dtypes.

### Consequences

These force internal callers to bypass `Index.take` and work on the underlying arrays directly:

- **`frame.py` idxmin/idxmax**: `algorithms.take(index._values, ...)` instead of `index.take(...)`
- **`reshape/merge.py`**: appends a sentinel value to the index, with a comment: *"We do not use allow_fill and fill_value because it throws a ValueError on integer indices"*
- **`indexes/base.py` reset_index**: take-then-putmask as two operations
- **`io/formats/excel.py`**: guards `allow_fill` on `levels._can_hold_na`
- **`indexes/multi.py`**: `algos.take_nd(lev._values, ...)` instead of `lev.take(...)`

### Proposed fix

- Respect the caller's `fill_value`
- Remove the `_can_hold_na` gate (let the underlying array handle type promotion)
- Simplify the workaround sites

This is backward-compatible: the existing gate (`allow_fill=True` + `fill_value is None` → numpy-style take) is preserved, so bare `idx.take(indices)` is unchanged.

Separately, there are questions about the right long-term defaults for `allow_fill` (currently `True` for backward compat but arguably should be `False` to match `ExtensionArray.take`), but that would require a deprecation cycle and is out

The overall goal is reading vertically stacked CSV files, with multiple tables.

ExtensionArrays can define a `_values_for_json` method if the standard numpy array with `object` dtype returned by `__array__` is not serializable because the objects themselves are not serializable. However this method is only utilized for `DataFrame.to_json` trough `BlockManager.column_arrays`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/core/internals/managers.py#L1249-L1251

In `Series.to_json` no path leads to the `_values_for_json` method and nearly always `__array__` is utilized. Therefore some ExtensionArrays are only JSON serializable if they are in a `DataFrame` and not a `Series`, which in my opinion also could be considered a bug.

### Feature Description

In short modify the `objToJSON.c` file to also call `_values_for_json` for pandas `Series`.

With the help of GitHub Copilot I was able to trace the issue to the `get_values` function, specifically the following lines:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L201-L213

- In `201` we are effectively calling `Series.values` and assign it to `values`.
- If the `Series` and therefore `values` is not empty `values` now is a numpy array or ExtensionArray.
- Next in `205` it is checked if `values` has a `__array__` attribute and if so calls it, that is also the path mentioned above that leads potentially to the numpy array of object dtype with not serializable objects in it.
- At last in `210` if none of the checks above worked it is checked if `values` is already a `np.ndarray` (and only that, so no subclass) and if not dereferences `values` and tries to create the array somewhere up the stack (if I understand it correctly).

My proposal would be to add another check after the empty check

### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.assign.html

### Documentation problem

The current `DataFrame.assign()` documentation states that non-callable values such as a Series, scalar, or array are "simply assigned." However, it does not clearly explain that when a Series is passed, values are aligned by index labels rather than by position.

This behavior may be surprising to users, especially when compared to list or ndarray assignment, which is positional.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Add a short clarification and example demonstrating that:

- Series values are aligned by index labels
- Missing labels result in NaN values
- List/ndarray values are assigned positionally

### Issue Description

For example, `pd.bdate_range(end="20260320", periods=3)` correctly returns:

`['2026-03-18', '2026-03-19', '2026-03-20']`

title: ENH: Add coerce errors functionality to pandas.Series.apply
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I would like to use pandas.Series.apply without creating helper functions to coerce errors. 

Currently if I am applying a function to a series that I know could raise errors (for example, trying to make each item in series of strings into an int), I have to write a small helper function to coerce errors into None or other.

I would like pandas.Series.apply to have a new parameter called errors, with possible values of 'raise' and 'coerce', similar to pandas.to_datetime.


### Feature Description

Adds a new parameter to pandas.Series.apply, to coerce errors.

Pseudocode implementation:
```
def apply(self):
    func = self.func
    if self.errors == "coerce":
        def safe_func(val):
            try:
                return func(val)
            except Exception:
                return np.nan
        results = [safe_func(val) for val in self.values]
    else:
        results = [func(val) for val in self.values]
    return results
```

Example usage:
```
s = pandas.Series(['1', '2', 'N/A'])
s = s.apply(lambda x: int(x), errors = 'coerce')
```

### Alternative Solutions

Write helper functions when necessary:
```
def coerce_to_int(x):
    try: return int(x)
    except: return None
s = pandas.Series(['1', '2', 'N/A'])
s = s.apply(coerce_to_int)
```

This is viable but requires the user to write many helper functions.

title: BUG: mask(inplace=True) gives where() results in EA recursive path
body:
`DataFrame.mask(cond, other, axis, inplace=True)` produces incorrect results (equivalent to `where()`) when `other` is a Series with ExtensionArray values.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [4, 5, 6]})
ser = pd.Series(pd.array([7, pd.NA, 9]))
mask = np.ones(df.shape, dtype=bool)
mask[1, :] = False

df.mask(mask, ser, axis=0)            # correct: replaces rows 0, 2
df.mask(mask, ser, axis=0, inplace=True)  # wrong: replaces row 1 (where() semantics)
```

The cause is a double negation in `NDFrame._where`. `mask()` passes `~cond`, then `_where` negates again (`cond = -cond if inplace`) before reaching the EA recursive path at `generic.py:10095-10120`. The recursive `_where` calls are non-inplace, so they interpret the double-negated cond with where semantics, producing the wrong result.

The non-EA path (which goes through `putmask`) is not affected.

title: ENH: Proposal for pd.col() for multi-column and regex column selection
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

`pd.col()` currently only supports selecting a **single column**, even though its
behavior allows expressions to be chained in ways that naturally suggest
multi-column operations should also work.

The function is defined as:

```python
def col(col_name: Hashable) -> Expression:
```

Internally it constructs an `Expression` whose evaluation function does:

```python
def func(df: DataFrame) -> Series:
    if col_name not in df.columns:
        raise ValueError(...)
    return df[col_name]
```

This always returns a **Series**, meaning `pd.col()` is fundamentally
single-column oriented.

### Inconsistent behavior with lists

Passing a list currently does not raise a clear error:

```python
pd.col(["price", "discount"])
```

The expression is created successfully, but when evaluated it produces:

```python
df[["price", "discount"]]   # returns a DataFrame
```

This creates inconsistent behavior when chaining operations such as:

```python
df.assign(total=pd.col(["price", "discount"]).sum())
```

because the expression now operates on a **DataFrame instead of a Series**.
The behavior becomes unclear and differs from user expectations.

### Missing regex selection

There is currently no way to express pattern-based column selection inside
`pd.col()`:

```python
pd.col("^price_", regex=True)
```

This fails with:

```python
TypeError: col() got an unexpected keyword argument 'regex'
```

Users must instead rely on eager operations such as:

```python
df.filter(regex="^price_")
```

which breaks the composable expression style that `pd.col()` aims to provide.

### Summary of limitations

Currently `pd.col()` does **not support**:

- Multi-column selection
- Regex-based column selection
- dtype-based column selection
- Any expression whose base resolves to a DataFrame

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
df.columns = ["a", "a"]

df.plot.hist()
# TypeError: no numeric data to plot

df.plot.box()
# TypeError: no numeric data to plot
```

### Issue Description

Plotting a DataFrame with duplicate column names raises `TypeError: no numeric data to plot`, even when all columns are numeric.

The root cause is in `MPLPlot.__init__` ([core.py line 193-195](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/core.py#L193-L195)):

```python
self.columns = [
    col for col in data.columns if is_numeric_dtype(data[col])
]
```

When columns are non-unique, `data[col]` returns a DataFrame instead of a Series. `is_numeric_dtype` returns `False` for DataFrames, so all duplicate-named columns are silently dropped, leaving `self.columns` empty.

- `_ensure_frame` (line ~681): `data.loc[:, cols]` with duplicate names causes column expansion

title: DEPR: deprecate set_eng_float_format
body: Claude wrote this at my request. ## Proposal Deprecate `pd.set_eng_float_format()` in favor of using `pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(...))` directly. Human Update Or just deprecate without an alternative. I haven't seen any evidence that anyone uses this. ## Rationale `set_eng_float_format` is a legacy convenience function (added in v0.5.0) that is a thin wrapper around `set_option`: ```python def set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=False): set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy, use_eng_prefix)) ``` It is the only top-level `pd.set_*` function that exists outside the options API, making it an odd outlier in the public API. This was already identified in #15610, where the consensus was to integrate this into the options machinery or deprecate it. **Evidence of minimal usage:** - **GitHub code search** yields ~30 results for `set_eng_float_format` outside pandas-dev/pandas. The vast majority are vendored copies of pandas, type stubs, or re-exports (xorbits, modin, Apache Beam, pyparallel, pandas-stubs, etc.). Only **2** results are actual user code calling this function. - **Stack Overflow** has **zero** questions or answers mentioning `set_eng_float_format`. - **Only 2 bug reports** have ever been filed against this function in the pandas issue tracker (#11981 in 2016, #15610 in 2017). The replacement is straightforward and equally concise: ```python # Before pd.set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True) # After from pandas.io.formats.format import EngFormatter pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True)) ``` This keeps `EngFormatter` available (it is not being deprecated), removes a one-off top-level function that doesn't fit the options API pattern, and simplifies the public API surface. Closes #15610.

title: DOC: Fix incorrect Sphinx cross references in older, whatsnew restructred text files.
body:
The top level `doc/` directory contains [reStructuredText](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/restructuredtext/basics.html#rst-primer) files who's names will end in `.rst` and are used to build the pandas documentation using [Sphinx](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/index.html). These files can contain Sphinx [cross-referencing](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/referencing.html) syntax to create a link to where the reference is documented. Cross references should reference currently documented pandas objects or objects in other libaries specified in the `intersphinx_mapping` variable in `doc/source/conf.py`

When `sphinx-build` command is run with [`nitpicky = True`](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/configuration.html#confval-nitpicky) set in the `doc/source/conf.py`, the logs will specify the file location, line number, and invalid cross references. title: API: Add reduction methods to ExtensionArray subclasses
body:
The subclasses of `ExtensionArray` implemented within pandas can support various reductions, but many do not have specific reduction methods defined, e.g. `.mean()`. We should fill these out for better API consistency.

The only method that should be added to `ExtensionArray` itself is `count`, as this can be implemented for all EAs via `ExtensionArray.isna`.

I'm already working on this.

title: Double braces used in docs in `read_csv`
body:
**This is not sufficient.**

The issue appears in multiple places across the documentation (e.g., parameter descriptions and examples where {{ }} is rendered instead of { }). We should identify and fix the root cause or update all affected occurrences, otherwise the docs will remain inconsistent and continue to show invalid Python syntax in other sections.

Just in `reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html` ([link](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html)), there are at least:
- Double braces `{{ }}` appear in code examples instead of normal Python dict braces `{ }`, producing invalid syntax (e.g., `dtype={{"Value": float}}`).

- The `date_format` example also uses double braces:  
  `date_format={{"col 2": "%d/%m/%Y", "col 3": "%a %d %b %Y"}}`.

- Parameter type description for `dtype` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{Hashable dtype}}`.

- Parameter type description for `converters` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableCallable}}`.

- Parameter type description for `na_values` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableIterable}}`.

- Enum values for `engine` render incorrectly as:  
  `engine {{‘c’, ‘python’, ‘pyarrow’}}`.

- Enum values for `quoting` render incorrectly as:  
  `{{0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL, ...}}`.

- Header renaming description renders placeholders incorrectly as:  
  `".{{count}}"`.

- Placeholder examples for unnamed columns render incorrectly as:  
  `"Unnamed: {{i}}"` and `"Unnamed: {{i}}_level_{{level}}"`.

- Several dictionary examples throughout the page use `{{ }}` instead of `{ }`, which makes the shown Python code invalid.

_Originally posted by @smith558 in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64412#pullrequestreview-3902956455_

title: DEPR: float_precision in read_csv
body: We have "high" (the default), "legacy", and "round_trip". When it was introduced in #8044, using the "high" precision apparently came with a performance penalty, but that changed by 2017 (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/17154#issuecomment-319917647) so the default was changed from "legacy" to "high" in #36228. I can't think of any reason why anyone would use "legacy". I'm not aware of anyone who uses this parameter at all. Let's deprecate it and simplify the code+API. Update: I patched the code to always use precision="high" to see whether it broke any tests. Aside from a test specifically asserting that "legacy" is _inaccurate_, the only test that broke was `test_precise_conversion` (4 cases out of 42) where we parse `1.700000000000000177635684` to `1.7`. I'm fine with this level of rounding (though I think using `fast_float` might improve it to `1.7000000000000002` which is what pyarrow gives). I'd also be OK with saying "round_trip" level precision is only for the python engine (though that engine also gives 1.7)

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import tempfile, os

print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}")

idx = pd.date_range("2019-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="h")
print(f"Index dtype: {idx.dtype}")  # datetime64[us] in pandas 3.0

df = pd.DataFrame({"value": np.random.randn(len(idx))}, index=idx)
tmpfile = tempfile.mktemp(suffix=".h5")

df.to_hdf(tmpfile, key="test", mode="w", format="table")

with pd.HDFStore(tmpfile, mode="r") as store:
    # where query returns 0 rows (BUG)
    result = store.select("test", where="'index' >= '2020-01-01' & 'index' <= '2023-01-01'")
    print(f"With where: {len(result)} rows")  # 0 — wrong!

    # Without where + manual filter works fine
    all_data = store.select("test")
    filtered = all_data[(all_data.index >= "2020-01-01") & (all_data.index <= "2023-01-01")]
    print(f"Manual filter: {len(filtered)} rows")  # ~26305 — correct

os.unlink(tmpfile)
```

**Output (pandas 3.0.1):**

```

title: PERF: DataFrame.describe() calls Series.reindex() N times instead of once
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

When DataFrame.describe() processes a DataFrame with many columns, there's an inefficient pattern where Series.reindex() is called for each column.
```python
col_names = reorder_columns(ldesc)
d = concat(
    [x.reindex(col_names) for x in ldesc],  # reindex() called N times
    axis=1,
    ignore_index=True,
    sort=False,
)
```
With N columns, Series.reindex() is called N times. Instead of aligning the index individually for each Series, we can concat first and reindex the entire DataFrame once to achieve the same result.



``` python
import timeit
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def bench_describe(n_cols: int, n_rows: int = 100, repeat: int = 5) -> float:
    np.random.seed(42)
    df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(n_rows, n_cols))
    _ = df.describe()
    times = timeit.repeat('df.describe()', globals={'df': df}, number=3, repeat=repeat)
    return min(times) / 3 * 1000

for n_cols in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    print(f"{n_cols:>5} cols: {bench_describe(n_cols):>8.1f} ms")
```

title: Suggestion: link a RAG / LLM debugging checklist (WFGY Problem Map) in the docs
body:
Hi pandas team,

thank you for maintaining such a foundational library. pandas is often the first stop for people who are building data workflows that later feed into LLM or RAG systems (corpus cleaning, chunking, metadata enrichment, offline evaluation, and so on).

I maintain an MIT-licensed project called **WFGY Problem Map**, which is a 16-question diagnostic checklist for RAG / LLM pipelines in production. It focuses on data and retrieval failure modes (ingestion gaps, chunking pathologies, vector store issues, evaluation leaks, etc), not on model weights.

Why I think this might be relevant for pandas users:
- Many real-world RAG systems start from pandas DataFrames (documents, logs, event streams) before anything is embedded or indexed.
- Several of the 16 failure modes are about how tabular and semi-structured data are transformed and filtered before they reach a retriever.
- The checklist is tooling-agnostic and can be applied no matter whether people use pandas alone or in combination with other frameworks.

For credibility: the same checklist has already been included in a few curated / academic ecosystems such as
- ToolUniverse by Harvard MIMS Lab  
- Multimodal RAG Survey by QCRI LLM Lab  
- Rankify (University of Innsbruck)

Suggestion:

If you think it could be useful for your users, would you consider adding a small link in your docs or resource section such as

> “RAG / LLM debugging checklist: WFGY Problem Map (16 failure modes)”  
> https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY/blob/main/ProblemMap/README.md

Project home: https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY

Thanks again for all your work on pandas and for considering this small suggestion.

Best,  
PSBigBig

title: API: PeriodIndex(dt64_data) depends on container for data
body:
```
data = np.arange(5).view("M8[D]").astype("M8[ns]")
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(data)
assert dti.freq is None

pd.PeriodIndex(dti)             # <- raises bc no freq
pd.PeriodIndex(pd.Series(dti))  # <- infers freq="D" 
```

PeriodIndex goes through period_array -> PeriodArray._from_datetime64 -> dt64arr_to_periodarr.  When no freq is specified, this does

```
    if freq is None:
        if isinstance(data, ABCIndex):
            data, freq = data._values, data.freq
        elif isinstance(data, ABCSeries):
            data, freq = data._values, data.dt.freq
```

In the Series case we get `data.dt.freq`, which uses `inferred_freq` instead of `freq` (which is always `None` inside a Series).

I think we should consider this inconsistency a bug and always use data._values.freq.

title: PERF: loc/iloc setitem with list-of-lists unnecessarily round-trips through object array
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

When using `df.loc[:, cols] = value` (or df.iloc) with a 2D list-of-lists on a mixed-dtype DataFrame, two things happen that are unnecessarily slow:
1. np.ndim(value) constructs a temporary array just to check dimensionality
```
elif np.ndim(value) == 2:
    # TODO: avoid np.ndim call in case it isn't an ndarray, since
    #  that will construct an ndarray, which will be wasteful
    self._setitem_with_indexer_2d_value(indexer, value)
```
2. `_setitem_with_indexer_2d_value` round-trips through an object array
```
if not is_array_like(value):
    value = np.array(value, dtype=object)
# ...
for i, loc in enumerate(ilocs):
    value_col = value[:, i]
    if is_object_dtype(value_col.dtype):
        value_col = value_col.tolist()
    self._setitem_single_column(loc, value_col, pi)
```

For a list-of-lists, the full sequence is:
- np.array(value, dtype=object) — O(n) element-by-element boxing into Python objects
- value[:, i] — slice an object column
- is_object_dtype(...) → True
- value_col.tolist() — convert right back to a Python list

So the data goes list → object array → list for every column, which is pure waste.

Reproducible example

```
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import timeit

# Mixed dtypes force the split path where the issue occurs
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "a": np.zeros(1_000_000),

title: DOC: Clarify deprecation and removal of Substitution and Appender classes
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/util/_decorators.py

### Documentation problem

The `Substitution` and `Appender` classes are fully implemented but emit deprecation warnings. 
Currently, there is no clear documentation or guidance about when or how these classes will be removed. 

This may confuse new contributors who are trying to understand legacy code, as they may not know whether these classes should be used, maintained, or ignored.


### Suggested fix for documentation

Update the documentation or docstrings for the `Substitution` and `Appender` classes to:

1. Clearly indicate that these classes are deprecated.
2. Provide an expected timeline or version when they will be removed.
3. Optionally, suggest alternatives if applicable.

This will reduce confusion for new contributors, improve clarity, and make the codebase easier to maintain.

title: BUG: test_assignment_not_inplace incorrectly xfailed due to wrong assertion
body:
@jbrockmendel asked [claude] to open this.

## Summary

`tests/computation/test_eval.py::TestOperations::test_assignment_not_inplace` is marked `xfail` with reason `"Unknown: Omitted test_ in name prior."` The test was previously named without a `test_` prefix so pytest never collected it. When it was renamed, it started failing — but the failure is due to a bug **in the test itself**, not in pandas.

## The bug

The test checks that `df.eval("c = a + b", inplace=False)` does **not** modify `df` in place. However, the final assertion compares `df` (2 columns) against `expected` (3 columns, including `"c"`):

```python
actual = df.eval("c = a + b", inplace=False)
expected = df.copy()
expected["c"] = expected["a"] + expected["b"]
tm.assert_frame_equal(df, expected)  # wrong: compares `df` instead of `actual`
```

This assertion would only pass if `df` *was* modified in place — the exact bug the test was meant to guard against (GH#9297).

## Fix

- Remove the `xfail` marker
- Replace `tm.assert_frame_equal(df, expected)` with `tm.assert_frame_equal(actual, expected)`
- Add a check that `df` is unchanged, e.g. `assert list(df.columns) == ["a", "b"]`

title: DOC: Redundant and misspelled command in docs
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/doc/source/development/contributing.rst

### Documentation problem

There is a typo/redundancy in these lines of code describing how to create a fork
```
git fetch upstream
get fetch upstream --tags
```

1. The first part of the issue is that the last line has a typo (`get` instead of `git`, and I can confirm the command failed when I tried to run it). Fixing the typo on the second line one would get
```
git fetch upstream
git fetch upstream --tags`
```
2. The second part of the issue is that when the typo is fixed, the first line becomes redundant, since the second line fetches everything the first one fetches and also fetches the tags.

### Suggested fix for documentation

One can replace the two lines above with a single one without typos and achieve the same result
```
git fetch upstream --tags`
```

title: PERF: `DataFrame.merge(sort=False)` slow for unsorted single-key integer joins when other side is sorted/unique and range-like

### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

``` python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import time

def bench(label, fn, repeat=3):
    times = []
    for _ in range(repeat):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    print(f"{label:35s} best={min(times):.4f}s  median={np.median(times):.4f}s")

n = 1_000_000
step = 2

left_sorted = pd.DataFrame({"k": np.arange(n, dtype=np.int64), "v": 1})
right_sorted = pd.DataFrame({"k": np.arange(0, n, step, dtype=np.int64), "w": 1})

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
left_unsorted = left_sorted.iloc[rng.permutation(n)].reset_index(drop=True)

bench(
    "left join sorted baseline",
    lambda: left_sorted.merge(right_sorted, on="k", how="left", sort=False),
)

body:
### Pandas version checks

### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.case_when.html


### Documentation problem

The description in the doc string does not make clear the semantics of the method. I felt I had to stare at the example for too long to determine the semantics. I don't come from a SQL background and am not familiar with `CASE WHEN`.

Reading the example

```python
>>> c = pd.Series([6, 7, 8, 9], name="c")
>>> a = pd.Series([0, 0, 1, 2])
>>> b = pd.Series([0, 3, 4, 5])
```

```python
c.case_when(
    caselist=[
        (a.gt(0), a),  # condition, replacement
        (b.gt(0), b),
    ]
)
```

I expected the output to be

```python
0    6
1    3
2    4
3    5
Name: c, dtype: int64
```

As if the series of masks were applied and it takes the last. It was not until I read up on what `CASE WHEN` is that it more clicked.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Add description that row replacement stops at first condition that is `True`.

title: BUG: unique().item() query no longer possible since unique() method no longer returns array
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.__version__
# '3.0.0'
df = pd.DataFrame([
  {"person": "John", "userName": "Johnny1234"}, 
  {"person": "Jane", "userName": "Jane3"}
])
person = df.query("userName == 'Johnny1234'")['person'].unique().item()

# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
# AttributeError: 'ArrowStringArray' object has no attribute 'item
```

### Issue Description

`unique` series method now returns array type rather than a series of unique items, breaking the use of .unique().item(), see discussions https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/18262#issuecomment-546746982 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/29250

Previously the use of the method would allow one to query a column with the expectation that only one result was returned. If none or more were returned, .item() would return a value error. 

The workaround for now is to do rewrap the array in a series object

```
person = pd.Series(df.query("userName == 'Johnny1234'")['person'].unique()).item()
```

### Expected Behavior

We would expect the following response
```
# 'John'
```

title: PERF: Avoid drop_duplicates(keep=False) in DataFrame.__getitem__ for single-column access
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

Observed (before fix): With n = 1000000 columns, 1000 accesses can take on the order of several seconds because each access builds a new Index via drop_duplicates(keep=False).

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/frame.py#L4162-L4169


```code
import pandas as pd
import timeit

# DataFrame with many columns and duplicate names; one column "key" appears once
n = 1000000
cols = ["a"] * (n - 1) + ["key"]
df = pd.DataFrame(0, index=range(10000), columns=cols)


# Repeated single-column access (e.g. in a loop or pipeline)
def access():
    for _ in range(100):
        _ = df["key"]


# Current state: each df["key"] calls columns.drop_duplicates(keep=False) → O(n) + allocation

sec = timeit.timeit(access, number=10)
print(f"1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): {sec:.2f}s")
```

Output

```
1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 8.69s
```

Expected: Single-column access when the key appears once should not rebuild the Index on every access; runtime should be much lower (e.g. well under 1 second for 1000 accesses).

Suggested Fix

```
if not is_mi:
    try:
        loc = self.columns.get_loc(key)
        if isinstance(loc, int):
            return self._get_item(key)
    except (KeyError, InvalidIndexError):
        pass
elif is_mi and self.columns.is_unique and key in self.columns:
    return self._getitem_multilevel(key)
```

Output would be

```
1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 0.04s
```

title: BUG: Different result from str.find depending on dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
examples=['ga',
          'Áa',
          '永a',
          '🐍a']
for t in examples:
    objects = pd.Series([t], dtype=object)
    strs = pd.Series([t], dtype=str)
    print('python:', t.find('a'), 
          'pandas with object type:', objects.str.find('a')[0],
          'pandas with string type:', strs.str.find('a')[0],          
          )
```

### Issue Description

`str.find` appears to be indexing its result based on bytes rather than characters. In the example, the basic python `str` type, and a `Series` using the `object` `dtype`, `find('a')` is `1` for all the example strings, as expected. With a `Series` using the new `str` `dtype`, the result is 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively. Note that encoded in UTF-8, Á takes two bytes, 永 takes three, and 🐍 takes four, so I suspect it's counting bytes instead of characters. `len` gives a result of 2 regardless of dtype.

### Expected Behavior

The result of `str.find` shouldn't change depending on dtype.

title: ENH: add `pd.col` to `pd.DataFrame.case_when`
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I suggest `pd.case_when` to support `pd.col` expression - the expression can be evaluated to either booleans or expected output within the case_when function : 

```py
data = {'name': ['Jason', 'Molly', 'Tina', 'Jake', 'Amy'], 
        'age': [42, 52, 36, 24, 73], 
        'preTestScore': [4, 24, 31, 2, 3],
        'postTestScore': [25, 94, 57, 62, 70]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data, columns = ['name', 'age', 'preTestScore', 'postTestScore'])
df
    name  age  preTestScore  postTestScore
0  Jason   42             4             25
1  Molly   52            24             94
2   Tina   36            31             57
3   Jake   24             2             62
4    Amy   73             3             70

caselist=[(pd.col('age').lt(10), 'baby'), 
          (pd.col('age').ge(10) & pd.col('age').lt(20), 'kid'), 
          (df.age.ge(20) & df.age.lt(30), 'young'), 
          (df.age.ge(30) & df.age.lt(50), 'mature'), 
          (df.age.ge(50), 'grandpa')]

df.assign(elderly = df.age.case_when(caselist=caselist))
    name  age  preTestScore  postTestScore  elderly
0  Jason   42             4             25   mature
1  Molly   52            24             94  grandpa
2   Tina   36            31             57   mature
3   Jake   24             2             62    young
4    Amy   73             3             70  grandpa
```

### Feature Description

within the `case_when` code, the pd.col expression is evaluated on the current dataframe, everything else stays as is

### Alternative Solutions

there isn't an alternative option at the moment. using pd.col makes things a bit cleaner. We can also leave things as is.
